lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: Okay, so how much can we really trust what psychology studies claim to prove?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: That is the core question in Estimating the reproducibility of psychologicalscience. The team wanted to check if results hold up when others repeat the exact work.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: So they just asked people to redo old experiments and see what happens?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Not quite. They actually ran one hundred replications using high powered designs and original materials whenever possible.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: High powered? Does that mean they had lots of participants to find tiny effects?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Exactly right. High powered designs give a better chance to detect the real effect size without noise.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: Okay, and what did they find when they compared the new results to the old ones?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: They found replication effects were only half the magnitude of original findings. That is a substantial drop.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: Half? So if the first study said an effect was strong, the second one says it is weak?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Yes. Ninety seven percent of original studies showed significant results but only thirty six percent did so in replications.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: That sounds like a lot of original findings were probably just lucky guesses.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: It is possible. Only forty seven percent of original effect sizes fell inside the ninety five percent confidence interval of replication results.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: And did any experts just look at the numbers and say they match up?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Some did. Thirty nine percent of effects were subjectively rated as replicating the original result by the judges.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: So even with all this failure, is there any good news in the whole report?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Yes. If we assume no bias and combine original plus replication results, sixty eight percent still have statistically significant effects.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: Okay, but what else explains why some studies work and others do not?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Correlational tests suggest replication success depended more on the strength of original evidence rather than team characteristics.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: So strong evidence in the first place matters most for getting a true replication.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Right. Strong original evidence predicts better outcomes than who runs the study or where it is published.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: Thanks Rowan, I think I understand why psychology needs more rigorous checks now.
